samples.text:
Nowadays many people only read news or watch programmes which agree with their own opinions. This essay will explain the reasons for this behaviour and the effects which it has on society.

There are several reasons why people do this. The first reason is that it is more comfortable. When people read something that agree with their ideas, they feel happy and confident, but when they read the opposite opinion they feel angry or uncomfortable. Secondly, social media and websites use algorithms which show users the same kind of news that they clicked before. For example, if someone like a political party and reads about it online, the website will show him more articles supporting this party. Also, many people are busy and they do not have time to search for different sources, so they just follow the news channel their family always watched.

This habit has several negative effects on society. Firstly, people become more extreme in their opinions because they never hear other sides of the argument. Secondly, society becomes divided into groups who do not understand each other and they argue a lot, especially on the internet. For instance, during elections, supporters of different parties often insult each other online instead of discussing. Moreover, it is easier for fake news to spread, because people believe any information that support their view without checking it.

In conclusion, people choose news which match their opinions because it feels comfortable and because of algorithms and lack of time. This makes society more divided and helps fake news to spread. I think people should try to read news from different sources to have more balanced view.

With a vast range of news sources now available, many people choose to consume only those that confirm their existing beliefs. This essay will explain why this tendency has become so common and discuss its effects on society, which I believe are largely harmful.

One key reason is psychological. People naturally prefer information that supports what they already think, because it makes them feel intelligent and secure, while opposing views can cause discomfort or even anger. The structure of the modern media landscape strengthens this tendency. Social media platforms and news apps use algorithms to recommend content similar to what users have previously clicked on, so a person who reads one article with a particular political slant will be shown many more like it. In addition, some news outlets deliberately target an audience with a clear political identity, since loyal viewers who share their outlook are commercially valuable.

The consequences for society are serious. First, when individuals are only exposed to one perspective, their opinions tend to become more extreme, as they rarely meet persuasive counter-arguments. This contributes to political polarisation, in which different groups not only disagree but regard each other with suspicion or hostility. Public debate suffers as a result, since it becomes difficult to reach compromise on important issues like climate policy when each side has different facts. Second, selective consumption helps misinformation spread more easily, because people are less likely to question a false story if it fits what they want to believe. Some argue that like-minded communities give people a sense of belonging, but this benefit hardly outweigh the damage to social cohesion.

In conclusion, people choose news that reflects their opinions because it is psychologically comforting and because algorithms and media companies encourage it. This leads to polarisation, weaker public debate and the rapid spread of misinformation.
samples.why: Clear position with both questions answered and extended · coherent paragraphs with a clear central idea · good range of vocabulary (political slant, polarisation, social cohesion) · frequent error-free sentences with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
The modern media landscape offers an almost unlimited choice of news sources, yet many people use this freedom to confine themselves to outlets that echo what they already believe. This behaviour has deep psychological roots and is reinforced by technology, and its effects on society are, in my view, predominantly damaging.

At the most basic level, people seek out confirming information because it is reassuring. Having one's views validated produces a sense of certainty and belonging, whereas encountering strong counter-arguments can be unsettling and may even feel like a personal attack. This natural bias is amplified by the design of digital platforms. Recommendation algorithms are optimised for engagement, and since users tend to click on content that aligns with their views, they are fed a steady diet of similar material until alternative perspectives effectively disappear from their screens. Commercial incentives play a role as well: news organisations have discovered that cultivating a loyal audience with a distinct ideological identity can be more profitable than attempting to appeal to everyone.

The social consequences are significant. When citizens inhabit separate informational worlds, they lose not only a shared set of opinions but also a shared set of facts, which makes productive debate extremely difficult. Views tend to harden, since they are rarely tested against opposing evidence, and people increasingly regard those who disagree not as fellow citizens with different priorities but as ignorant or malicious. This polarisation can paralyse decision-making on complex issues that require compromise. Furthermore, echo chambers provide fertile ground for misinformation, because claims that flatter a group's assumptions are shared eagerly and seldom checked.

In conclusion, selective news consumption stems from a desire for reassurance, reinforced by algorithms and commercial strategy. Its effects, including polarisation, the erosion of common ground and the spread of falsehoods, pose a real threat to healthy public discourse.
samples.why: Both questions answered with a clear, sustained position · ideas developed with precise cause-effect reasoning · sophisticated vocabulary used naturally (validated, inhabit, fertile ground) · wide range of error-free complex structures.
